To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) first degree stochasticdominance is a sufficient condition for stochastic dominance in multi samplingenvironments, (2) the sufficient condition is necessary if individuals are risk averse, and (3) the sufficient condition may not be necessary if individuals are “extremely” risk averse.
(i) the dominance criterion is first degree stochastic dominance and (ii) the upper bound on risk-aversion is zero, for any environment that permits sampling.
(1) stochastic dominance in multi sampling is first degree stochastic dominance; and (2) stochastic dominance in sampling environments is identical to that in nonsampling environments.

the effects of sampling on the stochastic dominance relations between random variables.
the question of how the sampling environment alters the stochastic dominance ordering of random variables.
the effect of sampling rules on the stochastic dominance criterion.

stochastic dominance is not a very useful concept in sampling environments.
stochastic dominance is a useful criterion for ranking random variables in sampling environments.
the dominance criterion for sampling environments is first degree stochastic dominance for any degree of risk aversion.

the sampling environments do not alter the stochastic dominance ranking of random variables.
stochastic dominance is a very strong criterion for sampling environments.

the sampling process is a key determinant in the choice of a dominance criterion.
